canonical_concept.beeja: अ (A) — the first letter of the Sanskrit alphabet, representing the unmanifest source. In the Gītā (10.33), Kṛṣṇa declares "akṣarāṇām akāro'smi" — among letters I am the letter A.
canonical_concept.vyakarana: Ātman is a masculine noun (though it refers to the genderless Self). Derived from the root at (to move) or an (to breathe). The word appears in all cases and is used reflexively ("oneself"). Pāṇini treats ātman as a reflexive pronoun in certain constructions.
canonical_concept.functional_meaning: Ātman is the eternal, unchanging Self underlying individual existence. It is the witness (sākṣī) of all mental and physical activity, never itself modified. The Upaniṣads teach that Ātman is not the body, not the mind, not the intellect, not the ego — it is the pure awareness in which all these appear. The realization of Ātman as identical with Brahman (Aham Brahmāsmi) is the goal of Advaita Vedānta.
canonical_concept.dhatu: अत् (At) — To move constantly; also connected to अन् (An) — to breathe, to live.
canonical_concept.nirukta: Yāska: "ātmā vyāpnoti iti" — that which pervades. Also: "ātmā aniti prāṇiti" — that which breathes. The Self is both the pervader and the life-breath.
canonical_concept.tattva: Ātma-Tattva — the principle of pure consciousness and selfhood. In Advaita: Ātman is identical with Brahman (Aham Brahmāsmi). In Sāṃkhya: Ātman (Puruṣa) is pure consciousness, eternally distinct from Prakṛti. In Viśiṣṭādvaita: Ātman is real but eternally dependent on and part of Brahman-Viṣṇu.

claims.value: In Advaita Vedānta (Śaṅkara): Ātman = Brahman; the apparent difference is due to avidyā (ignorance). The mahāvākyas (great sayings) express this identity: "Aham Brahmāsmi," "Tat tvam asi," "Prajñānam Brahma," "Ayam Ātmā Brahma." In Sāṃkhya: Ātman (Puruṣa) is one of infinite individual consciousnesses, eternally distinct from Prakṛti. In Viśiṣṭādvaita: Ātman is real, individual, and eternally a part (aṃśa) of Brahman-Viṣṇu. In Dvaita (Madhva): Ātman is eternally distinct from Brahman; five eternal distinctions (pañca-bheda) are real.

provenance.source_text: Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.18-20 (Ātman as the rider in the chariot)

claims.value: In Purāṇic cosmology: the individual ātman (jīvātman) is a spark of the universal Paramātman. The ātman transmigrates through the fourteen lokas according to karma. In Sāṃkhya cosmology: Puruṣa (Ātman) is the passive witness; Prakṛti (matter) evolves the universe for Puruṣa's experience and eventual liberation.

provenance.source_text: Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.18-20 (Ātman as the rider in the chariot)

claims.value: Ātman is the deepest layer of the self, beyond the five koshas (sheaths). In Yoga psychology: the ātman is the sākṣī (witness) that observes the modifications of the mind (citta-vṛttis) without being affected. The goal of yoga is to still the mind so the ātman shines in its own nature (svarūpa). The Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad describes four states of consciousness (waking, dreaming, deep sleep, turīya) and identifies Ātman with the fourth state (turīya) that underlies all three.

provenance.source_text: Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.18-20 (Ātman as the rider in the chariot)

claims.value: The concept of ātman in governance: the ruler who recognizes the ātman in all beings governs with compassion and justice. The Arthaśāstra's concept of rāja-dharma is grounded in the king's recognition of his own ātman and its reflection in all subjects. Aśoka's transformation after Kalinga was described in terms of recognizing the ātman in the suffering of others.

provenance.source_text: Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.18-20 (Ātman as the rider in the chariot)

claims.value: In Āyurveda: the ātman is the ultimate cause of life (jīvana-hetu). Disease occurs when the ātman's connection to the body is disturbed. The concept of ātma-jñāna (self-knowledge) is considered the highest medicine. Caraka Saṃhitā states that the physician who knows the ātman can heal at the deepest level.

provenance.source_text: Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.18-20 (Ātman as the rider in the chariot)

claims.value: The concept of ātman in mathematics: the Upaniṣadic teaching "ekam evādvitīyam" (one without a second) is the mathematical statement of non-duality. The concept of infinity (ananta) in Indian mathematics is connected to the infinite nature of Ātman-Brahman. Zero (śūnya) in Indian mathematics represents the void from which the ātman emerges.

provenance.source_text: Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.18-20 (Ātman as the rider in the chariot)

claims.value: In Jyotiṣa: the Sun (Sūrya) is the cosmic symbol of Ātman — the self-luminous source of all light. The Sun's position in the birth chart (Sūrya-rāśi) represents the ātman's expression in this life. The concept of Sūrya as Ātman appears in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

provenance.source_text: Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.18-20 (Ātman as the rider in the chariot)

claims.value: In alchemical traditions (Rasaśāstra): gold (suvarṇa) is the metal of the ātman — pure, unchanging, self-luminous. The alchemical goal of transmuting base metals to gold mirrors the spiritual goal of realizing the ātman beneath the base ego.

provenance.source_text: Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.18-20 (Ātman as the rider in the chariot)

claims.value: The Upanayana (sacred thread ceremony) initiates the student into the knowledge of Ātman. The Mahāvākya "Tat tvam asi" is transmitted from teacher to student as the core teaching. The Śrāddha ritual is based on the belief in the ātman's continuity after death. The Ahaṃgrahopāsanā (meditation on "I am Brahman") is the primary ātman-realization practice.

provenance.source_text: Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.18-20 (Ātman as the rider in the chariot)

claims.value: The flame (dīpa) symbolizes Ātman — self-luminous, unaffected by wind (worldly disturbances). The sky (ākāśa) symbolizes Ātman's all-pervading, uncontained nature. The mirror symbolizes the mind reflecting the ātman's light. The lotus in the heart (hṛdaya-puṇḍarīka) is the seat of the ātman in Upaniṣadic symbolism.

claims.value:
- Ṛgvedic period: Ātman primarily means "breath" or "life-force"
- Atharvaveda: Ātman begins to acquire the meaning of "self"
- Early Upaniṣads (Bṛhadāraṇyaka, Chāndogya): Ātman = Brahman identity established
- Middle Upaniṣads (Kaṭha, Muṇḍaka): Ātman as the inner controller (antaryāmin)
- Later Upaniṣads: Ātman doctrine fully systematized
- Śaṅkara (8th century CE): Advaita interpretation — Ātman = Brahman
- Rāmānuja (11th century CE): Viśiṣṭādvaita — Ātman as part of Brahman
- Madhva (13th century CE): Dvaita — Ātman eternally distinct from Brahman
